name: Iris A/B: counter-scale vs clip-path
summary: A device test for an iris that opens from a ballot oval. The left pane scales a round window up while scaling the photo inside it down by the inverse (two Web Animations, transform only, so the compositor runs them). The right pane animates clip-path: circle(), which Safari and most browsers repaint on the main thread. Turn on Busy main thread to burn 12ms of every frame: the transform iris keeps its pace while the clip-path iris stutters. The drift readout shows how far the photo inside the counter-scaled window wanders between keyframe samples, and Ratio-bounded places keyframes so no two neighbours differ by more than 6% in scale, which keeps drift under a tenth of a percent. Open this on the real phone; the frame gaps shown are main-thread gaps.
api: mask: scale(s)  media: scale(1/s) about the focal point · keyframe whenever s changes 6% · drift = (r−1)²/4r · clip-path: circle(r at fx fy) for comparison

name: Interruptible film scrub
summary: A four-chapter film on one Web Animations clock (push, iris, ink flood) with a chapter rail you can drag. Pressing the rail pauses every animation and hands the playhead to a critically damped follower, so dragging feels smooth even when the pointer jitters, and a fast flick coasts a little further. Releasing resumes playback only if the film was playing. Only animations whose scene overlaps the playhead get currentTime written each frame, which keeps a long film cheap to scrub. Chapter clicks can glide or cut; arrow keys step a second, Home and End jump to the ends.
api: down: pause all, target = x→ms · frame: cur += (target − cur)(1 − e^(−18dt)); a.currentTime = cur for live scenes · up: target += v·0.15, resume if was playing

name: Focal iris
summary: The next photo opens in a circle centred on its own subject, starting 10% large and settling, while the current photo pushes in 5% toward that same point and dims; reversing closes the iris into the subject. Use it when the subject matters more than the place, like portraits, products or a featured story.
api: next.clip = circle(R·p at focus(next)); next.scale = 1.1 − .1p; prev.scale = 1 + .05·pNext about focus(next)

name: Depth wipe
summary: The current photo slides off like a sheet and uncovers the next one behind it. The new photo travels less than the sheet’s edge, and its ground travels further than its sky, the parallax of a camera trucking sideways; a soft shadow from the sheet’s edge falls on it. Use it for places seen in order, like a travel story or a property tour, where direction means moving on.
api: edge = p; next.x = dir·(.2 + .3·nearness(y))·(1 − p); prev.x = −dir·(.12 + .2·nearness)·p

name: Blinds
summary: Vertical slats turn one after another, starting on the side you swiped from: each face narrows and darkens as it turns away while the new face widens. A fast flick turns the slats almost together; a slow drag spreads the wave out. Use it when photos are browsed by hand, like a lookbook, and the gesture should be felt in the change.
api: slat j: lp = (p − order(j, dir)·σ)/(1 − σ); σ = .52 − .05·|release velocity|; face width = lp

name: Develop
summary: The new photo arrives by brightness, highlights first and shadows last, the way a print comes up in the developer tray: undeveloped areas pale toward paper, and each area gains its colour after its tone. Use it when the frame stays in the same place and only the moment changes, like before and after or a time-lapse.
api: arrive(px) = (p − .55·(1 − blurredLum(px)))/.45; colour = mix(grey, rgb, arrive − .3); veil = .58·sin πp·(1 − arrive)

name: Rack focus
summary: Focus pulls off the current photo, which softens and breathes 4% larger like a real lens, while the next photo sharpens from its foreground back to its horizon. Use it to move attention between related shots, like a detail and the wide view, without implying a direction.

name: Horizon split
summary: The photo parts along its own horizon, the next caption shows in the seam, the seam slides to the new photo’s horizon, then the halves close on the new photo, which drifts in from the side of travel. Exit, then enter, never overlapping. Use it for chaptered stories, where each photo opens a new section.
api: open = tri(p); seam = lerp(horizon(from), horizon(to), ss(.3,.7,p)); content = from → to at p = .5

name: Tile wave
summary: The next photo grows in as dots that open into squares, in a wave that starts exactly where you clicked, tapped or started your swipe; keys start it from the side you are heading to. Use it when the change comes from a place the person pointed at, like choosing a hotspot or a map region.
api: tile: lp = (p − .56·dist(tile, pointer)/maxDist)/.44; square = ss(lp)·cell, radius = (1 − ss)·cell/2

name: Page turn
summary: The photo lifts from its right edge along a softly bowed fold: its back shows through, mirrored and washed like thin paper, and a shadow runs along the fold onto the next page. Going back lays the page down again. Use it for sequences people read in order, like a lookbook, a catalogue or a printed story.
api: fold.x = W(1 − q); tilt = .1·sin πq; flap = mirror(page right of fold)·scaleX(.58) + paper wash; shadow along fold

name: Relight
summary: The same scene moves from midday to afternoon to golden hour along a light front that spreads out from the sun’s path, sky before ground; stepping to another place falls back to a plain dissolve so the light front only ever means “same place, new light”. Use it when only the time or the conditions change, like a lighting preview or a day-to-evening product shot.
api: arrive(px) = (p − .62·dist(px, sun) − .14·ground(px))/.24; other scene: alpha = ss(0, 1, p)

name: Thumbnail to hero
summary: The thumbnail you choose lifts out of the strip and grows into the hero along a curved path: it rises first, then widens as it lands, while its slot stays outlined until it arrives and the old hero dims beneath. Use it for galleries with a visible strip or grid, so people see where the big photo came from.
api: rect = { cx: lerp(th, hero, p), cy: lerp(th, hero, 1 − (1 − p)^1.8), size: lerp(th, hero, p^1.25) }

name: Ink edge
summary: The next photo spreads in from the side of travel behind a calm, low-frequency ink contour that drifts slowly as it advances, with a faint darker rim like wash drying on paper. Use it for slower editorial pacing, where a hard wipe would feel mechanical.
api: contour = .74·travel(x) + .42·(fbm(x·1.8 + drift(p)) − .5); reveal where contour < mix(−.16, 1.1, p); rim darkens 16%

name: Fly-to strip
summary: The view pulls back in proportion to how fast it is travelling, slides along the strip and settles back in, so a jump of five photos shows more of the set than a step of one, and dragging lifts it slightly so neighbours peek in. Use it when position in the set matters, like chapters or numbered steps.
api: pos.set(i); zoom = 1 − min(.44, .1·|d pos/dt|^.85); view = translate(center − pos·(W + gap)·zoom) scale(zoom)

name: Momentum filmstrip
summary: The strip follows the pointer 1:1. On release the velocity is projected about 0.4 s ahead and the strip settles on the nearest frame edge from that same velocity, so a hard flick travels several frames and a nudge moves one. Past either end it rubber-bands and the scroll bar shortens. Inspired by Keen Slider free-snap and Flickity freeScroll; changed: frames keep their real aspect ratios and the counter reports the range in view. Use when photos come in mixed formats and people skim them fast, like a contact sheet.
api: target = nearest edge(x + v·0.42); x.release(x, min(v, ω·d), target)   bar.w −= overscroll

name: Inner parallax slides
summary: The frame follows the finger 1:1 while its photo drifts the other way inside it, and the caption runs slightly ahead, so three depths separate as you drag. The dot plate stretches from its leading edge and the trailing edge catches up. Inspired by Swiper parallax and Codrops slideshows; changed: every offset is computed from the slide’s distance to center, so it holds mid-flick, in reverse and when interrupted. Use when each slide is a place or a story and a sense of depth helps it read as a window.
api: d = (i·step − x)/step;  photo.x = −clamp(d)·0.22w;  caption.x = d·44;  plate = stretch(x/step)

name: Center-focus rail
summary: Each print scales and fades only by its distance from center, and spacing is integrated from that same scale curve, so gaps stay even and nothing rotates or overlaps. The caption under the center crossfades by distance while you drag. Inspired by Keen Slider’s distance-driven slides and Apple TV shelves; changed: positions come from integrating the scale, so the center print moves exactly 1:1 under the pointer. Use when one item is the subject and its neighbours are context, such as a print shop or a plan picker.
api: d = (i·step − x)/step;  s = 1 − .16·min(|d|,1) − .08·clamp(|d|−1);  pos = ∫₀ᵈ s(u) du · step

name: Swipe deck
summary: The top card follows the pointer 1:1 and tilts with its offset, toward the half you grabbed. Release projects position plus velocity: past 40% of the card it is thrown off at its own speed, otherwise it settles home without overshoot. The next card rises first and the rest of the stack follows 45 ms apart. Undo brings the last card back from the side it left. Use when every item needs a quick yes or no, such as triage, shortlists or review queues.
api: score = x + vx·0.15;  |score| > 0.4w ? x.release(x, vx, ±off) : x.release(x, cap(vx), 0);  depth[k].set(k, t + k·45ms)

name: Stories with hold to pause
summary: Segments fill from the clock. Holding anywhere pauses at once and, after 300 ms, fades the chrome so the photo can be read. A tap on the left third goes back, anywhere else goes forward, with an exit-then-enter swap; each photo drifts slowly while its segment runs. Inspired by Instagram stories; changed: pausing, holding and time spent off screen are all subtracted from one start time, so the bar never jumps. Use when short, ordered moments should play hands-free but stay under the viewer’s control.
api: e = (frozen ? tp : t) − t0;  fill[cur] = e/5;  unfreeze: t0 += t − tp;  e ≥ 5 → next

name: Synced thumbnail rail
summary: The main photo drags 1:1. The thumbnail plate is a pure function of that position: its leading edge reaches the next thumb first and its trailing edge follows, so it stretches mid-move in either direction and can never drift out of sync. The rail recenters on the active thumb and can be flicked on its own. Inspired by Swiper thumbs and Flickity asNavFor; changed: one position drives both, instead of two carousels messaging each other. Use when people compare similar photos and need detail and overview at once, such as product galleries.
api: p = x/step;  [a, b] = stretch(p, thumbL, thumbR);  rail.settle(center(thumb[round p]))

name: Infinite loop
summary: Each slide is placed modulo the loop length from one unbounded position, so the track never resets, velocity carries across the seam and a flick can be caught anywhere. Across the seam the dot indicator drains out of the last slot while it fills the first, so it never jumps back across the row. Autoplay steps every four seconds and holds while hovered or focused. Inspired by Embla’s slide looper; changed: placement is computed per slide, never by cloning or teleporting the track. Use when a set has no natural end, such as postcards, testimonials or logos.
api: rel = ((i·step − x) mod L + 1.5L) mod L − L/2;  seam: dot[n−1] drains as dot[0] fills

name: Peek and pull shelf
summary: Cards align to the left margin and the next one peeks in, so a phone screen always shows there is more. Dragging past the last card rubber-bands into a ring that fills with the stretch; past the mark the label swaps to Release, and letting go opens the full list as a sheet while the shelf settles back. Inspired by the App Store and Airbnb shelves; changed: the “see all” target lives inside the overscroll instead of a separate button. Use when a horizontal shelf sits inside a vertically scrolling phone screen.
api: pull = band(x) − max;  ring = pull/52;  release: pull > 52 → sheet.set(1); x.release(x, v, max)

name: Before and after lens
summary: The divider tracks the pointer exactly; a tap on the photo glides it to the tap and then tracks 1:1, and a fast release carries it a little further without overshoot. While held, the knob opens into a 2.25× lens centred on the seam, so both lights can be compared at the same pixel; on touch the lens floats above the finger. It is a real slider: arrows, Shift, Page keys, Home and End, and Enter or Magnify keep the lens open. Inspired by Juxtapose and the iOS text loupe. Use when two aligned images differ in detail, such as edits, relights, or before and after.
api: x = held ? pointer + catch(t) : x.at(t);  lens: L = 40 + 108·open, zoom = 1 + 1.25·open;  after.clip = inset(0 0 0 x)

name: Vertical reel
summary: Vertical drag is 1:1 and a flick moves at most one reel, like Reels and Shorts; captions trail their photo slightly so the move reads as depth. Pulling up past the last reel fills a ring; released past the mark, the next four are appended and the same release velocity carries straight into the first of them. The arrow keys and buttons do the same, including loading the next set. Use when each item fills a phone screen and people move through them one at a time.
api: i = clamp(nearest(y + v·0.2), i₀ ± 1);  pull > 60 → append(4), y.release(y, v, (n₀)·h)

name: Masonry row carousel
summary: Photos keep their exact aspect ratios: tall ones span both rows and wide ones pair up in a column whose width makes both fit exactly. The rail free-scrolls with momentum and snaps to column edges; selecting shrinks the photo inside its frame and fills the check. Tab walks every photo and the rail follows focus. Inspired by Google Photos’ justified grid; changed: packed by column so it scrolls sideways. Use when portrait and landscape photos must be picked quickly without cropping them.
api: pair w = (H − g)/(1/a₁ + 1/a₂);  tall w = H·a;  target = nearest column(x + v·0.4)

name: Route-linked carousel
summary: The carousel position is the hiker’s place on the trail: the marker, the inked part of the route, the clock and the mile counter are all computed from the same scroll value, and each stop’s photo is lit for its hour, warming from midday to golden hour. Dragging the marker along the map scrubs the carousel, and arrow keys step stop to stop on either one. Inspired by Strava route replays and Apple Maps guides; changed: the map is a second handle on one rail, not a separate view. Use when slides happen in a place or in sequence and showing where you are matters, such as itineraries, tours or timelines.
api: p = x/step;  marker = path[k].at(f·len);  dashoffset[k] = len·(1 − clamp(p − k));  clock = lerp(time[k], time[k+1], f)

name: Grid to lightbox, shared element
summary: Press a tile and that same photo grows out of it: position, size, crop and corner radius all spring from the tile to the viewer, while the grid behind it dims. The caption and controls arrive only after the photo is most of the way there. Stepping to the next photo is a Swap, so the old one leaves in the direction of travel before the new one arrives. Closing runs the controls out first, then flies the photo back into whichever tile it ended on. Use when a grid of thumbnails needs a viewer that keeps the user oriented.
api: photo.rect.set(open ? fit : tileRect); scrim.set(1); chrome.set(1, delay .16); step: exit 100ms, then enter from dir*40px

name: Swipe down to dismiss
summary: Open a photo and drag it anywhere: it follows the pointer one to one and shrinks about the point you hold as you pull down, while the scrim fades with the distance and the controls fade out within the first 70 pixels. On release the pointer velocity decides: a fast flick or more than a fifth of the height hands the photo to the shared-element flight back to its tile, keeping the finger speed, and anything less springs back to centre. Use when a viewer needs the natural, touch-first way out.
api: photo = fit + finger; scale = 1 − .42·pull; scrim = 1 − dy/(.55H); release: proj = dy + vy·.22 > .2H ? flyTo(tile, vy) : settle(0, vy)

name: Lightbox with pinch, wheel and double-tap zoom
summary: The photo is a transform, not a layout: two fingers scale it about their midpoint while the midpoint drags it, a double-tap zooms to the exact point tapped, and Ctrl plus wheel (a trackpad pinch) zooms about the cursor without taking over normal scrolling. Pull past an edge and the image resists on a rubber band that grows harder the further you go; let go and a critically damped spring returns it, carrying the flick as glide that stops at the edge instead of bouncing off it. A locator in the corner shows which part you are looking at. Switching photos is a Swap that resets the zoom while the picture is invisible. Use when photographs need inspecting at pixel level.
api: view = {s, x, y}; release: s → clamp(1, 5), x → glide(x + v/ω, ±bound(s)); tap², wheel: x′ = f − (f − x)·s′/s

name: Filterable masonry that reflows
summary: Choosing a subject runs three beats in order. Photos that no longer match shrink to their own centre in 100ms, staggered 20ms apart. Then the photos that stay travel to their new slots on a soft spring, one every 30ms in reading order so the reflow sweeps rather than jumps. Last, photos that now match grow in from their own centre, 200ms in. The pill behind the active filter is a two-edge indicator (leading edge first, trailing edge 60ms behind) and the count rolls its digits. Use when a gallery filters in place and people should keep track of what moved where.
api: leave: s→0 (snap, k·20ms) · stay: x,y→slot (soft, 80ms + k·30ms) · enter: s→1 (base, 200ms + k·35ms) · height.set(newH)

name: Collection to collection morph
summary: Twelve photographs are one set of elements that every collection arranges differently: a lead image with a grid, a plain grid, justified rows, tall columns. Switching runs in order. Photos not in the next collection shrink away first. Photos that are in both travel to their new slots, re-cropping as they go (a landscape becomes a tall column without a jump cut), starting 80ms later and staggered by their new position. Photos that are new to the collection grow in last. The title swaps on the same schedule: out, then in. Use when albums, smart collections or saved sets share photos and the user should see what carried over.
api: next = layout(kind, ids); leave: s→0 · stay: rect→next (soft, k·30ms) · enter: s→1 (200ms+) · title: swap

name: Contact sheet with a loupe
summary: A round loupe follows the pointer on a snap spring, so it trails the hand by a few frames instead of being glued to it. What it shows is the sheet itself, scaled 3.4 times about the lens centre, so frames cross the glass continuously and picks you have marked show up inside it. The lens pops in on enter and out on leave, and its label swaps (out, then in) as the centre crosses from one frame to the next. On touch the lens sits above the finger so it is never hidden by it; from the keyboard it parks on the focused frame. Use when people must judge sharpness or expression across many small frames without opening each one.
api: lens.xy.set(pointer, snap); content = sheet·scale(3.4) translated so lens centre = sheet point; label.swap(frameUnderLens)

name: Photo stack that fans out
summary: Seven prints sit in a loose pile, each tilted a few degrees. Hover (or tap) and the top print leaves first, then each one beneath it 35ms later, all swinging out about the base of the pile into an arc. The print under the pointer lifts along its own axis while its neighbours lean away from it, and which print that is comes from the angle to the base, not from what is under the cursor, so a lifting print never flickers. Pick one and it travels to the top of the pile as the rest close from the bottom up. Use when a collection needs a compact, tactile preview that opens in place.
api: fan: card.f.set(1, delay (n−1−slot)·35ms) · hover: lift along local axis, neighbours rotate ±3° · pick: slot→top, f.set(0, delay slot·25ms)

name: Hover-focus grid
summary: The photo under the pointer stays exactly as it is and gains a small caption. Every other photo quietly drains of colour, dims and settles back 3.5 percent, and it does so in a wave: the nearest neighbours go first, the far corner last, about 14ms per 100 pixels. Moving to another photo retargets the same springs, so nothing restarts. Leaving the grid returns everything on the slow spring, over about half a second. Click or tap pins the focus so touch screens and keyboards get the same state; Escape releases it. Use when a portfolio grid should direct attention without hiding the rest.
api: hover(i): others.r.set(1, soft, delay d(i,j)·.14ms/px) · i.r.set(0) · leave: all.r.set(0, lazy) · r → saturate, brightness, scale

name: Caption and metadata drawer
summary: The drawer is one number, how far it is open, and everything reads from it. The drawer rises on a soft spring (or follows your finger one to one on its handle, and release velocity picks open or closed); the photo, 50ms behind it, slides up and shrinks just enough that the marked subject ends 16px above the drawer’s top edge, and not a pixel more. Turn on the subject marker to see the area it protects. Detail rows then fade up one after another as the drawer passes each threshold. Changing photo is a Swap, and the new photo gets its own subject maths. Use when a lightbox needs captions and EXIF without covering what the picture is about.
api: open ∈ [0,1]; photo.y = lerp(y₀, y₁, open), y₁ = min(y₀, H − D − 16 − subject.bottom·s); s = min(1, (H − D − 16 − top)/subject.bottom)

name: Cull deck: keep or reject by throwing
summary: The top photo follows the pointer one to one and tilts with how far it has travelled, while the photo beneath it rises and grows by exactly the same amount, so the deck advances as you pull rather than after you let go. Let go and the throw is judged by where it was heading: distance plus a fifth of a second of velocity. A keep carries your speed into a flight that shrinks and re-crops the photo into the next empty slot of the tray. A reject leaves on the other side and fades. Undo returns the last photo along its own path, and the tray slot empties. Keys do the same with no velocity. Use when a shoot has to be sorted quickly and every decision should leave a visible trace.
api: pos = index + clamp(|dx|/.55w); card(i).depth = max(0, i − pos); release: |dx + vx·.2| > .38w ? fly(tray slot | off-edge, vx) : return(0, vx)

name: Pinned hero zoom-out
summary: Use when a landing page should open on one striking detail and then reveal the whole image. The photo starts zoomed to the lit ridge and full bleed; scrolling pulls the camera back (log-scale zoom) while the window shrinks into a framed print with rounded corners. Only after the zoom settles do the three headline lines rise out of their masks, 8% of scroll apart, then the caption. Reduced motion shows the framed end state and fades the lines in.
api: p = (y − top)/(3H − H)   e = sine(p/.78)   s = s0^(1−e)   clip = lerp(viewport, frameRect, e)   line[i].y = (1 − (p − .5 − .08i)/.18)·110%

name: Pinned horizontal gallery
summary: Use when a short run of related photos sits inside a long page and a carousel would hide them behind buttons. The section pins while the row has travel left: each pixel scrolled down moves the row one pixel left, smoothed by the follower. Inside every card the photo drifts against the travel by up to 10% of its width (depth), the progress line fills, and the counter changes as a card crosses the centre. Reduced motion keeps the 1:1 travel and drops the inner drift.
api: x = −p·(trackW − W)   img[i].x = −(cx[i] − W/2)/W·.18·cardW   bar.scaleX = p   section.h = H + travel

name: Stacking cards
summary: Use when an ordered process of three to five steps should replace one step with the next while the earlier ones stay visible. Cards pin 12px apart; as the next card rises over one, that card scales down from its top edge (5% per card above it) and dims, so the stack recedes in depth while its edges stay readable. Coverage is computed from the next card’s distance to its own pin, so scrolling back lifts them out in reverse. Reduced motion keeps the dimming and drops the scale.
api: cover[i] = 1 − ((top[i+1] − y) − pin[i+1])/(cardH + gap − 12)   depth[i] = Σ cover[j≥i]   card.scale = 1 − .05·depth   dim = .14·depth

name: Clip window to full bleed
summary: Use when a page should move from editorial text into an immersive photo without a hard cut. The photo sits behind a small rounded window; scrolling opens the clip-path toward full bleed with the top and bottom edges leading and the sides lagging 8% of scroll behind, while the photo eases from 1.18× to 1×. The headline rides the top edge out, the note rides the bottom edge, and the caption tag fades in last. Reduced motion cuts from window to full bleed at the midpoint.
api: ev = ease(p/.6)  eh = ease((p − .08)/.6)   clip = inset(lerp(t0,0,ev) lerp(l0,0,eh) … round lerp(14,0,eh))   img.scale = lerp(1.18, 1, ev)

name: Chapter scrollytelling
summary: Use when each block of a narrative has its own picture: a case study, a trip, a product tour. Text steps scroll on the left while the photo pins on the right (on phones the photo pins full height and the steps scroll over it as cards). The photo holds while a step is centred, then in the gap between steps the next photo rises from below through a mask while the old one drifts up 18%, both tied to scroll so it reverses exactly. The caption swaps (exit, then enter) at the midpoint and the active step brightens. Reduced motion cross-fades.
api: f = i + (focus − c[i])/(c[i+1] − c[i])   q = ease((frac(f) − .3)/.4)   next.clip = inset((1−q)·80% 0 0 0)   next.y = (1−q)·20%   prev.y = −q·18%

name: Parallax depth planes
summary: Use when a hero should feel spatial without 3D assets. One PhotoKit scene is cut into planes in the page: per column, flat runs are found from the bottom up and clustered into ridge tones; the sky is the back plane. Scrolling moves each plane by its depth (sky 8%, far ridge 25%, near slope 100% of a 16% range), and the headline sits between the far and middle ridges, so it rises from behind the hills. Reduced motion holds the planes still and fades the headline in.
api: planes = split(PhotoKit.get(ridge))   plane[k].y = (.5 − p)·.16H·depth[k]   headline: z between plane 1 and 2, y = lerp(.62H, .2H, ease(p/.6))

name: Relight as you read
summary: Use when the photo should keep pace with long-form reading: an essay, a case study, a place. As you read, the city relights from noon to golden hour. The warm exposure arrives as a soft band sweeping from the sun’s corner (top right) toward the bottom left, so light visibly travels across the scene; the time tag counts with it and the paragraph being read brightens. Reduced motion replaces the sweep with an even cross-fade.
api: p = y/(scrollH − H)   golden.mask = linear-gradient(225deg, #000 (p·150 − 35)%, transparent (+35)%)   clock = lerp(12:10, 19:35, p)

name: Scroll-scrubbed sequence
summary: Use when a product or place reveal should feel like video but stay under the reader’s control. 24 frames are generated from one PhotoKit scene with the sun sinking (tod 0 → 1), lazily and nearest-to-the-playhead first. Scroll position is the playhead: the follower-smoothed index picks two neighbouring frames and blends them by the fraction between, so slow scrolling never steps. The tick rail and clock follow the same index. Reduced motion shows the nearest frame without blending.
api: i = p·(N − 1)   draw(frame[floor i]); alpha = frac(i); draw(frame[ceil i])   frames generated one per render, nearest first

name: Chapter rail with gentle snap
summary: Use when readers of a long guide or documentation page jump between sections. The rail shows every chapter with a bar that fills as you read it (one bar per chapter, sized to its length); clicking a chapter glides there on a soft spring. Snap is off by default; when on, it waits until you have stopped scrolling for 180ms and only pulls if a chapter start is within 22% of the view, so it settles rather than grabs, and any wheel, touch or key cancels it. Narrow, the rail becomes a segmented bar across the top. Reduced motion jumps.
api: fill[i] = clamp((y + .3H − c[i])/(c[i+1] − c[i]))   idle > 180ms && |c[k] − y| < .22H ⇒ glide.set(c[k], S.soft)   input ⇒ glide.cancel()

name: Contact sheet to print
summary: Use when a case study or portfolio piece should show the edit, not just the result. Three acts on one pinned sheet: a loupe travels the contact sheet frame by frame in reading order and settles on the keeper (0–32%); a grease-pencil box draws around it (32–46%); then the sheet pushes in around that frame and fades while the frame itself grows into the full-bleed print, so the print visibly comes from its cell (46–92%), and the caption arrives last. All of it is scrubbed by scroll. Reduced motion cuts between the three states.
api: loupe = path(cells[0..PICK], ease(p/.32))   mark.dash = (p − .32)/.14   e = sine((p − .46)/.46)   print = lerp(cellRect, viewport, e)   sheet.scale = lerp(1, 1.6, e) about cell[PICK]

name: Progressive photo load
summary: A blurred 0.6 KB placeholder holds the layout from the first frame. When the real file lands it develops like a print in the tray: shadows come up first, then midtones, highlights last, over one second. Cached photos skip the reveal entirely, because animating something already there reads as lag. Use when: a feed, gallery or hero loads large photos over slow networks and the layout must not jump.
api: a(px) = smoothstep(0, .3, dev·1.32 − (0.85·lum + 0.15·grain))   dev = (t − arrival)/1.1s; cached ⇒ dev = 1

name: Hover rack focus
summary: Depth comes from the photo itself: each tree row is a flat tone and farther rows are hazier, so luminance sorts into planes. Point anywhere and focus pulls to that plane on a slow critically damped spring while the reticle tightens; blur everywhere else scales with distance from the focal plane and the aperture. Use when: a hero or product shot should guide the eye to what the pointer or the copy is talking about.
api: focus.set(depth(pointer), S.lazy)   blur(px) = |depth − focus| · aperture · maxR   (36-tap gather, occlusion-aware)

name: Brand tint to colour
summary: Every photo is gradient-mapped through three tokens (darkest neutral, a tint, lightest neutral), so mixed sources read as one set in both themes. The story under the pointer or keyboard focus cross-fades back to full colour on a soft spring; switching the tint dissolves old map into new. Use when: a grid mixes photos from many sources and needs one calm brand look, with colour reserved for the item you are on.
api: duo = gradientMap(lum, [dark, tint, light])   card.colour.set(hover || focus ? 1 : 0, S.soft)

name: Relight with the sun
summary: Two pixel-aligned exposures of the same ridge, midday and golden hour, blend through a soft light mask centred on the sun: light near the sun warms first, the far side last. Drag the sun along its path (1:1, then it coasts on release velocity) and it sets behind the real ridge line. Use when: a hero photo should follow the visitor’s local time or the mood of a page, without shipping a second photo set.
api: mask = g + (pool(sun) − .45)·.7·sin(πg)   colour = mix(day, golden, mask)   sun drawn on sky only; g.release(g, v·dg/dpx)

name: Depth parallax
summary: The photo is split into planes by aerial perspective (farther ridges are lighter). The pointer offsets each plane by its depth around a pivot at the middle ridge: sky and far ridge drift against the pointer, the foreground follows it, at most about 1% of the width. Planes ride a lazy spring and drift home when the pointer leaves. Use when: a landing hero needs a sense of place without video, and the photo must stay fully readable.
api: q = s + off·(depth(q) − .4)  (4 fixed-point steps)   off.{x,y}.set(pointer·amt, S.lazy)

name: Halftone to photo
summary: The hero arrives as print: an ink screen whose dot sizes carry the photo’s tones in the page’s own ink and paper colours. It then resolves over 2.2 s: the screen gets finer, the dots take on the photo’s colour, and the last stretch dissolves into the full photograph. Scrub it, or pick dots or a 15° line screen. Use when: an editorial or campaign hero wants a printed, considered entrance that still ends on the real photo.
api: cell = c0·(1.4/c0)^smoothstep(0,.9,p)   dot r = √(coverage/π)   out = mix(screen, photo, smoothstep(.62,1,p))

name: Grade with live histogram
summary: Exposure and white balance are applied in linear light, and the same curve runs on a 1/8-size copy to draw the histogram, so the graph slides with the photo as you scrub. Drag sideways on the photo for exposure, or use the sliders. Auto exposes to the right (the 98th percentile lands just under white) with half a grey-world balance; Auto and Reset glide there on a soft spring. Clipped highlights and crushed shadows can be painted in danger and accent. Use when: people adjust uploads in a media library or editor and need to see what they are losing.
api: lin = srgb^2.2 · wb(T) · 2^EV   hist = Σ LUT(px)   ev.set(auto, S.soft) | ev.jump(slider)

name: Paint in colour
summary: A soft brush paints the colour photo through a black-and-white print. Every cell of the mask stores when it was painted, so the heal is a pure function of time: it holds for 1.4 s, then the colour drains back over 2.6 s, and painting again resets the hold. Reveal all opens from the centre outward. Use when: a story or campaign hero invites people to explore, or to show what a restoration or colourisation changed.
api: cell = { a0, ts, tp }   m(t) = a0 · ramp(t − ts) · heal(t − tp − 1.4s)   colour = mix(mono, photo, smoothstep(.08,.6,m))

name: Face-safe Ken Burns
summary: Each photo carries a focal box (the face, or the subject). The planner works out the largest zoom that still contains the box at this frame’s aspect ratio, then pans and zooms between two valid framings over seven seconds, clamping every frame so the face is never cut. If the frame is too wide even at full size, it zooms out over a blurred extension of the same photo instead of cropping the head. Slides cross-fade for 1.2 s while still moving. Use when: a hero slideshow or story cover animates portraits that must survive phone, tablet and desktop crops.
api: zMax = min(1.16, cropW/boxW, cropH/boxH)   centre = clamp(lerp(a0,a1,ease(u)), box ∩ image)   Pause meets WCAG 2.2.2

name: Fade flicker compare
summary: Blink comparison without the flash: versions dissolve in linear light over about 200 ms, so brightness never dips mid-fade and the eye still catches what moved. Hold Space or press on the photo to peek at the other version; Flicker alternates every 1.2 s until stopped; Difference paints only what changed. The version label swaps (exit, then enter) in step. Use when: reviewers approve an edit, a re-export or a new version and the change is subtle.

name: Agent behaviours
summary: One agent performs eighteen behaviours inside a small web page, each a short loop that ends where it began. It hops to get around and every landing squashes and recovers without bouncing. What it carries trails its body and tilts against the motion. It leans into whatever it pushes, and its face changes mood brows first, then lids, then mouth. The page answers on the same clock: a button squashes, an outline snaps leading edge first, a pin goes in, text is struck through. Asking permission waits for your real Allow or Deny.

name: Agent duet
summary: Two agents and Maya’s cursor work one checkout page. The review agent lifts its lens to the total, the outline snaps around it, and it plants a pin. It turns to the fix agent, they catch each other’s eye, and the note flies across on a spring. The fix agent hops over, its pencil nudges the total back into line, and the reviewer watches and smiles. Maya’s cursor comes in, both agents look up at it, and her click resolves the pin. They hop, staggered. Drag either agent to interrupt: the other stops to watch, and once it lands they pick up the beat they were on.

name: Agent mark concepts
summary: Five agent marks drawn from Arc’s own vocabulary instead of a generic sparkle: a turning arc, the review tool’s lens, the orbit eye, the path and the invitation frame. Each shows its brand form (paper tile, one wash, 1.7 ink line) and its product form at 32, 24 and 16px as a square outline that inherits text colour. Working turns on each mark’s own motion. Picking a card updates the presence chip, pin and byline below so you judge it in context.

name: Agent mark states
summary: The agent mark carried through seven agent states. Thinking turns the arc at a constant speed; Browsing sends a square marker along the equator while the arc leans toward it; Commenting grows the review tool’s comment tail so the mark doubles as a pin; Waiting stands the arc upright and opens the invitation corners; Done and Error morph the equator’s five points into a check or an X. Every change is a critically damped spring, and the same drawing runs at brand size, 32, 24 and 16px and inside the presence chip.

name: Agent character
summary: One agent on a floor. Its eyes follow your pointer anywhere on the page, with the face sliding a beat later like a head turning. Pick an expression and the brows move first, then the lids, then the mouth, then the body settles. Click it and it squeezes, hops and smiles; drag it 1:1 and let go to throw it, and it leans into the throw, stretches as it flies, the antenna trails behind, and the landing squash recovers without bouncing. Idle, it breathes, blinks, glances and now and then fidgets. The 24, 48 and 96px copies mirror it frame for frame.

name: Agent crowd
summary: Five agents with different washes idle on one floor: each breathes, blinks and fidgets on its own clock, and every few seconds one glances at a neighbour; when two catch each other’s eye they both smile. The research agent is thinking, so its arc keeps turning. They look at your pointer while it moves. Throw one and every agent it passes turns to watch it, looks surprised, leans away, then goes back to what it was doing; the sleepy one wakes up for a while. Landing on someone makes them shuffle aside.

name: Agent cast: checkers and writers
summary: Twelve role agents stand in a lineup, all the same species (one square body, one face, one arc antenna) and each with its own prop, habit and default mood. Each idles in character: the stopwatch ticks, the caret staff blinks, the speech bubble swaps scripts, the glasses creep down, and every few seconds one of them plays its signature action. Tap one and its neighbours lean away and turn to watch, staggered outward from it; the agent on stage hops back to its place first, then the chosen one jumps forward, growing as it flies, lands with a squash, and plays its signature. Its name, job and habit swap in as it takes off. Props trail the body on lagging springs, hanging parts swing a beat late and settle without swinging back, and every eye follows your pointer.

name: Agent cast: operate and people roles
summary: Twelve role characters on one rig stand in a row, each idling in character: the scheduler checks its ticking watch, support nods while it listens, the designer draws a square in the air that lingers then fades, the developer types on keys that dip, the archivist lifts its box lid and lets it settle. Tap one and the others step back in a ripple from the one you chose while it hops forward and lands with a squash; then its name and job swap in, it switches to its action mood and plays its signature move. Props trail the body on lagging springs, so every hop, lean and landing carries through them. On a phone the row scrolls sideways with snap above the focused stage.

summary: An email-scoped palette where rows spring into slots as you type, the highlight trails on lagging edges, and the preview swaps behind the pick.

summary: Recipient chips open width-first and the text fades in after. Bad addresses flag danger with a message; good ones settle into a success check terminal.

summary: Vote bars fill with a base stagger while percents fade in lazy. The pick keeps its check, the tally rolls its digits, and votes can move.
